claims.claim: IPs are mainly located in the subventricular zone (SVZ).
claims.source: IPs are mainly located in the subventricular zone (SVZ) (Kowalczyk et al., 2009; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kowalczyk et al., 2009 and Paridaen and Huttner, 2014.

claims.claim: Early-born neurons give rise to deep cortical layers (V and VI) and late-born neurons form superficial layers (II–IV).
claims.source: This migration occurs in an inside-out manner, in which early-born neurons give rise to deep cortical layers (V and VI) and late-born neurons form superficial layers (II–IV) (Molyneaux et al., 2007; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Shibata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Molyneaux et al., 2007; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; and Shibata et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Disruption of NPC genomic integrity during embryonic development causes increased NPC apoptosis, reduced neuron production, and neuron mislocalization, ultimately resulting in decreased cortex size or microcephaly.
claims.source: Disruption of NPC genomic integrity during embryonic development causes increased NPC apoptosis, reduced neuron production, and neuron mislocalization, ultimately resulting in decreased cortex size or microcephaly (McKinnon, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to McKinnon, 2013.

claims.claim: The rapid proliferative activity of NPCs imparts a high degree of endogenous replication stress and DNA damage.
claims.source: The rapid proliferative activity of NPCs imparts a high degree of endogenous replication stress and DNA damage, which can lead to the formation of excess single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Harley et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012; McKinnon, 2017; O'Driscoll, 2017; Reynolds et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Harley et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012; McKinnon, 2017; O'Driscoll, 2017; and Reynolds et al., 2017.

claims.claim: ATM and ATR kinases play independent and essential roles in DDR, and their loss can lead to neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration.
claims.source: ATM and ATR kinases play independent and essential roles in DDR, and their loss can lead to neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017; Madabhushi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017 and Madabhushi et al., 2014.

claims.claim: ATM can be activated by DSBs in both NPCs and immature neurons, while ATR is responsible for G2/M checkpoint induced by RPA-bound ssDNA during replication stress in proliferating NPCs.
claims.source: ATM can be activated by DSBs in both NPCs and immature neurons, while ATR is responsible for G2/M checkpoint induced by RPA-bound ssDNA during replication stress in proliferating NPCs (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017.

claims.claim: DNA DSB repair by homology-directed repair (HDR) is prevalent in mitotically active NPCs, and non-homologous end joining becomes the pathway for DNA repair in postmitotic neurons.
claims.source: DNA DSB repair by homology-directed repair (HDR) is prevalent in mitotically active NPCs, and non-homologous end joining becomes the pathway for DNA repair in postmitotic neurons (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017; Madabhushi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017 and Madabhushi et al., 2014.

claims.claim: ATR and ATM act through their respective downstream targets CHEK1 and CHEK2 to activate p53-mediated cell cycle arrest or apoptosis if DNA damage remains unrepaired.
claims.source: ATR and ATM act through their respective downstream targets CHEK1 and CHEK2 to activate p53-mediated cell cycle arrest or apoptosis if DNA damage remains unrepaired (Sengupta and Harris, 2005; Shaltiel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Sengupta and Harris, 2005 and Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Depletion of SMC5 at early stages of mouse brain development resulted in reduced cerebral cortex size due to mitotic abnormalities in NPCs, perturbed differentiation, and increased apoptosis.
claims.source: In this study, we show that depletion of SMC5 at early stages of mouse brain development resulted in reduced cerebral cortex size due to mitotic abnormalities in NPCs, perturbed differentiation, and increased apoptosis, which collectively affected cortical layer formation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the study's findings and is supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claims.claim: SMC5 depletion leads to genome instability and DDR activation.
claims.source: We observed that SMC5 depletion leads to genome instability and DDR activation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 2 and 5.

claims.claim: The cortex size of Smc5 cKO mice was restored upon knockout of Trp53 or Chek2 genes.
claims.source: We found that the cortex size of Smc5 cKO mice was restored upon knockout of Trp53 or Chek2 genes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: SMC5/6 is important for DNA replication fork stability.
claims.source: Subsequently, using an auxin-inducible degron (AID) system to deplete SMC5 in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) we mimicked cell proliferation and cell death phenotypes observed in vivo, which were also rescued by inhibition of p53 or CHEK2. Using the AID system, we determined that SMC5/6 is important for DNA replication fork stability and propose a role for SMC5/6 in the processing of under-replicated DNA intermediates to ensure accurate chromosome segregation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Exon 4 of the Smc5 cKO allele was flanked by loxP Cre recombinase target sequences.
claims.source: Exon 4 of the Smc5 cKO allele was flanked by loxP Cre recombinase target sequences.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Depletion of SMC5 via Smc5 cKO has been shown to destabilize the entire SMC5/6 complex.
claims.source: Depletion of SMC5 via Smc5 cKO has been shown to destabilize the entire SMC5/6 complex (Gaddipati et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Nestin-Cre is expressed throughout the central nervous system.
claims.source: Nestin-Cre is expressed throughout the central nervous system (Dubois et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Dubois et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Emx1-Cre expression is restricted to the mouse cerebral cortex.
claims.source: Emx1-Cre expression is restricted to the mouse cerebral cortex (Gorski et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Nestin-Cre and Emx1-Cre recombinases demonstrate robust expression in the mouse cortex at E12.5.
claims.source: Nestin-Cre and Emx1-Cre recombinases demonstrate robust expression in the mouse cortex at E12.5, and the use of either one to mediate Smc5 cKO was expected to result in a similar phenotype during cortex development (Insolera et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Insolera et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The protein levels of SMC5 and SMC6 were only partially diminished in E13.5 brains.
claims.source: Although we observed conditional mutation of Smc5 in E13.5 brains, the protein levels of SMC5 and SMC6 were only partially diminished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: The deletion in Smc5 was accompanied by a substantial reduction in SMC5 and SMC6 protein levels in E16.5 embryos.
claims.source: In contrast, the deletion in Smc5 was accompanied by a substantial reduction in SMC5 and SMC6 protein levels in E16.5 embryos (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A-C.

claims.claim: Some degree of DNA excision was also observed in kidneys and muscles in Smc5 cKO samples.
claims.source: Since Nestin is expressed in progenitor cells of tissues other than neural, some degree of DNA excision was also observed in kidneys and muscles in our samples (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Bernal and Arranz, 2018; Sakairi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, with citations to Bernal and Arranz, 2018 and Sakairi et al., 2007.

claims.claim: SMC5 depletion in the developing mouse cortex resulted in a significant increase in cleaved caspase 3 (CASP3)-positive cells in Smc5 cKO compared to controls in both E13.5 and E16.5 cortices.
claims.source: SMC5 depletion in the developing mouse cortex resulted in a significant increase in cleaved caspase 3 (CASP3)-positive cells in Smc5 cKO compared to controls in both E13.5 and E16.5 cortices (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The increase in the number of cells undergoing apoptotic DNA fragmentation was most pronounced in E16.5 cortices.
claims.source: The increase in the number of cells undergoing apoptotic DNA fragmentation was most pronounced in E16.5 cortices (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: The depletion of SMC5 in mESCs causes chromosome segregation defects during mitosis.
claims.source: We have previously shown that the depletion of SMC5 in mESCs causes chromosome segregation defects during mitosis (Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Hwang et al., 2017 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claims.claim: The percentage of NPCs undergoing abnormal mitosis with characteristic DNA bridges and lagging chromosomes at anaphase was elevated in Smc5 cKO compared to control.
claims.source: The percentage of NPCs undergoing abnormal mitosis with characteristic DNA bridges and lagging chromosomes at anaphase was elevated in Smc5 cKO compared to control (Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claims.claim: There was an increase in abnormal anaphase cells when comparing Smc5 cKO cortices from E13.5 to E16.5 (9% versus 38%, respectively).
claims.source: We observed an increase in abnormal anaphase cells when comparing Smc5 cKO cortices from E13.5 to E16.5 (9% versus 38%, respectively; Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Depletion of SMC5 in NPCs caused a significant increase in the number of anaphase cells with oblique division axis (<60°).
claims.source: Depletion of SMC5 in NPCs caused a significant increase in the number of anaphase cells with oblique division axis (<60°) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claims.claim: Tissue-specific depletion of SMC5 did not affect overall embryonic development and mice survived to adulthood without additional morphological abnormalities.
claims.source: Tissue-specific depletion of SMC5 did not affect overall embryonic development and mice survived to adulthood without additional morphological abnormalities.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations of the mice.

claims.claim: The difference in brain weight and cortex size in Smc5 cKO mediated by Nestin-Cre was significant at postnatal day 0/1 (P0/1) and became more prominent in adults (P55).
claims.source: The difference in brain weight and cortex size in Smc5 cKO mediated by Nestin-Cre was significant at postnatal day 0/1 (P0/1) and became more prominent in adults (P55) (Figure 1J–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1J–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claims.claim: Emx1-Cre-mediated Smc5 cKO also led to reduced brain weight and cortex size in newborn and adult mice compared to littermate controls.
claims.source: Emx1-Cre-mediated Smc5 cKO also led to reduced brain weight and cortex size in newborn and adult mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 1N,O and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–L).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1N,O and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–L.

claims.claim: A significant delay in the time taken to contact the adhesive in Smc5 cKO mice compared to control mice was observed, which is evidence of impaired sensory activity.
claims.source: We observed a significant delay in the time taken to contact the adhesive in Smc5 cKO mice compared to control mice, which is evidence of impaired sensory activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Smc5 cKO mice underperformed in the inverted screen test compared to control mice.
claims.source: Smc5 cKO mice underperformed in this test compared to control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Smc5 cKO mice displayed less forelimb use during vertical exploration compared to controls.
claims.source: Smc5 cKO mice displayed less forelimb use during vertical exploration compared to controls, as demonstrated by the elevated ratio of rears with no paws touching the cylinder wall and the reduced ratio of rears with two paws touching the cylinder wall (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claims.claim: The reduced cortex size mediated by SMC5 depletion results in impaired sensorimotor function in mice.
claims.source: Collectively, these behavioral tests revealed that the reduced cortex size mediated by SMC5 depletion results in impaired sensorimotor function in mice.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the behavioral tests.

claims.claim: Aged adult (P293/295) Smc5 cKO brains showed reduced cortex size and thickness, as well as decreased brain weight, compared to the control mice.
claims.source: Following conclusion of the sensorimotor assays, the aged adult (P293/295) Smc5 cKO brains were assessed and showed reduced cortex size and thickness, as well as decreased brain weight, compared to the control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H.

claims.claim: Smc5 cKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) accumulate RAD51 foci in the presence of replicative stress.
claims.source: We previously showed that Smc5 cKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) accumulate RAD51 foci in the presence of replicative stress (Gaddipati et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Gaddipati et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Analysis of E16.5 embryonic tissues revealed upregulation of RAD51 in the neural cortex of Smc5 cKO mice.
claims.source: Analysis of E16.5 embryonic tissues revealed upregulation of RAD51 in the neural cortex of Smc5 cKO mice (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: p53 is upregulated and activated in MEFs and mESCs following Smc5 cKO.
claims.source: We have previously demonstrated that p53 is upregulated and activated in MEFs and mESCs following Smc5 cKO (Gaddipati et al., 2019; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Gaddipati et al., 2019 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claims.claim: p53 activation is observed in the progenitor zone of E16.5 Smc5 cKO cortices.
claims.source: Similarly, we observe p53 activation in the progenitor zone of E16.5 Smc5 cKO cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Brain weight was not affected in mice that were Trp53 KO alone.
claims.source: Brain weight was not affected in mice that were Trp53 KO alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The brain weight, cortex area, and cortical thickness size of Smc5, Trp53 double knockout (dKO) adult mice were comparable to littermate controls.
claims.source: The analysis of Smc5, Trp53 double knockout (dKO) adult mice revealed that the brain weight, cortex area, and cortical thickness size were comparable to littermate controls (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Significant differences were observed between Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5 cKO mouse brain parameters.
claims.source: However, significant differences were observed compared to Smc5 cKO mouse brain parameters (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Smc5 cKO in the mouse brain causes a p53-dependent apoptosis of neural cells.
claims.source: These data confirm that Smc5 cKO in the mouse brain causes a p53-dependent apoptosis of neural cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Adult Smc5, Chek2 dKO mouse brain weight, cortical thickness, and cortex area were significantly larger than Smc5 cKO mice.
claims.source: Indeed, adult Smc5, Chek2 dKO mouse brain weight, cortical thickness, and cortex area were significantly larger than Smc5 cKO mice (Figure 2B–D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The brain weight and cortex area of Smc5, Chek2 dKO mice were not restored to levels equivalent to the control or Chek2 KO mice.
claims.source: However, the brain weight and cortex area were not restored to levels equivalent to the control or Chek2 KO mice (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Abrogation of SMC5/6 functions results in DNA damage induced by DSBs and p53-mediated apoptosis likely through the ATM-CHEK2-p53 DDR signaling pathway.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that abrogation of SMC5/6 functions results in DNA damage induced by DSBs and p53-mediated apoptosis likely through the ATM-CHEK2-p53 DDR signaling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genetic rescue experiments.

claims.claim: The brain weight and cortex size of Smc5, Trp53bp1 dKO adult mice were not restored.
claims.source: Thus, we analyzed Smc5, Trp53bp1 dKO adult mice and revealed that the brain weight and cortex size were not restored (Figure 2D,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The loss of SMC5/6 complex functions induces a DDR independent of or epistatic with 53BP1-mediated signaling.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that the loss of SMC5/6 complex functions induces a DDR independent of or epistatic with 53BP1-mediated signaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the 53BP1 knockout experiments.

claims.claim: Increased DNA fragmentation was not evident in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO P0/1 cortices.
claims.source: In contrast to Smc5 cKO, increased DNA fragmentation was not evident in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO P0/1 cortices (Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Rescue of the cortex thickness defect caused by Smc5 cKO was observed when Trp53 or Chek2 are also mutated in P0/1 sagittal head cross-sections.
claims.source: From analysis of P0/1 sagittal head cross-sections, we observed rescue of the cortex thickness defect caused by Smc5 cKO when Trp53 or Chek2 are also mutated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: Depletion of SMC5 in the developing mouse cortex caused the displacement of apical NPCs marked by SOX2 and PAX6 into the area outside VZ.
claims.source: Depletion of SMC5 in the developing mouse cortex caused the displacement of apical NPCs marked by SOX2 and PAX6 into the area outside VZ (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Englund et al., 2005; Ferri et al., 2004; Sansom et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, with citations to Englund et al., 2005; Ferri et al., 2004; and Sansom et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The displacement tendency of apical NPCs was even more pronounced in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices.
claims.source: This tendency was even more pronounced in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: An increase in the total number of SOX2+ and PAX6+ NPCs was observed in both Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO compared to the control.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed an increase in the total number of SOX2+ and PAX6+ NPCs in both Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO compared to the control (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: A significant decrease in the number of TBR2+ IPs located in the SVZ of Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.
claims.source: In contrast to apical NPCs, we observed a significant decrease in the number of TBR2+ IPs located in the SVZ of Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control (Figure 3G–I; Arnold et al., 2008; Englund et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G–I, with citations to Arnold et al., 2008 and Englund et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The cortical area occupied by TBR2+ progenitors in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices was increased compared to the control.
claims.source: The cortical area occupied by TBR2+ progenitors in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices was increased compared to the control (Figure 3G–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Smc5 cKO leads to ectopic localization of NPCs and significant loss of IPs.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that Smc5 cKO leads to ectopic localization of NPCs and significant loss of IPs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the NPC and IP analysis.

claims.claim: Mutation of Trp53 or Chek2 in conjunction with Smc5 cKO alleviates the loss of IPs but exacerbates NPC ectopic localization.
claims.source: Mutation of Trp53 or Chek2 in conjunction with Smc5 cKO alleviates the loss of IPs but exacerbates NPC ectopic localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the double knockout analysis.

claims.claim: A significant decrease in TBR1+ (layer VI), CTIP2+ (layer V), and SATB2+ (layers II–V) cells in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.
claims.source: We observed a significant decrease in TBR1+ (layer VI), CTIP2+ (layer V), and SATB2+ (layers II–V) cells in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control (Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: The development of early- and late-born neuron populations were restored in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices.
claims.source: Assessment of the Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices demonstrated that the development of early- and late-born neuron populations were restored (Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: SMC5 depletion causes abnormal positioning of apical NPCs and reduction in the populations of IPs, as well as deep and upper cortical layer neurons.
claims.source: Taken together, SMC5 depletion causes abnormal positioning of apical NPCs and reduction in the populations of IPs, as well as deep and upper cortical layer neurons, suggesting a global impact on cortical development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the cortical development findings.

claims.claim: Absence of p53 and CHEK2 prevents the loss of IPs and restores cortical layer-specific neuron numbers.
claims.source: We also provide evidence that absence of p53 and CHEK2 prevents the loss of IPs and restores cortical layer-specific neuron numbers.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the double knockout analysis.

claims.source: Smc5 cKO cortical sections had 20.2% less Ki67+ proliferating and 35.7% less H3P+ mitotic cells compared to control (Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: A 34.7% decrease in CldU+ populations in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: There is an accumulation of cells in G1 phase of the cell cycle that are blocked from entering S phase in Smc5 cKO cortices.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Accumulation of two intensely stained H3P+ chromatin foci on both sides of the segregating chromosomes that also contained CldU was observed.
claims.source: Further, we observed accumulation of two intensely stained H3P+ chromatin foci on both sides of the segregating chromosomes that also contained CldU (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: No CldU signal was observed between either of the two intensely stained H3P+ foci.
claims.source: However, no CldU signal was observed between either of the two intensely stained H3P+ foci.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Increased number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO compared to control cells was observed, particularly at pericentromeric regions.
claims.source: In addition, we observed increased number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO compared to control cells, particularly at pericentromeric regions (Figure 4I–K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I–K.

claims.claim: The number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO cells was increased by 6.5-fold compared to control.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4J,K.

claims.claim: Pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci were increased by 8.1-fold in Smc5 cKO cells compared to control.
claims.source: The number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO cells was increased by 6.5-fold compared to control, while pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci were increased by 8.1-fold (Figure 4J,K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4J,K.

claims.claim: SMC5/6 components accumulate at pericentromeric heterochromatin regions of chromosomes.
claims.source: We have previously shown that SMC5/6 components accumulate at pericentromeric heterochromatin regions of chromosomes (Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claims.claim: A decrease in average width and intensity of pericentromeric H4K20 signal by 1.3- and 2.0-fold, respectively, in Smc5 cKO cells compared to control was observed.

results.result: Smc5 conditional knockout (cKO) in the developing mouse cortex causes neurodevelopmental defects characterized by increased NPC apoptosis, reduced cortex size, and impaired sensorimotor function. The phenotype is observed with both Nestin-Cre and Emx1-Cre drivers, with mice surviving to adulthood but exhibiting microcephaly and behavioral deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C34, C46-47, C52-59, C115, and C142 collectively demonstrate that Smc5 cKO causes increased apoptosis (CASP3+ and TUNEL+ cells), reduced brain weight and cortex size at multiple developmental stages (E13.5, E16.5, P0/1, P55, P293/295), and impaired sensorimotor function in behavioral tests. The data are consistent across multiple time points, Cre drivers, and assays, providing strong convergent evidence for the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

results.result: Smc5 cKO NPCs exhibit chromosome segregation defects during mitosis, including DNA bridges, lagging chromosomes, and oblique division axes. CldU labeling experiments reveal NPCs with under-replicated DNA entering mitosis, with intensely stained H3P+ chromatin foci on segregating chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C48-51, and C89-91 provide consistent evidence from multiple approaches (immunofluorescence of anaphase cells, CldU pulse-labeling) showing mitotic abnormalities in Smc5 cKO NPCs. The percentage of abnormal anaphase cells increases from E13.5 (9%) to E16.5 (38%), and the CldU labeling pattern suggests under-replicated DNA persisting into mitosis. The data are internally consistent and support the conclusion of chromosome segregation defects.

results.result: SMC5/6 depletion triggers a CHEK2-p53 DNA damage response pathway that mediates NPC apoptosis and cortex size reduction. Genetic deletion of Trp53 or Chek2 rescues the Smc5 cKO neurodevelopmental phenotype, while deletion of Trp53bp1 does not, indicating the DDR is independent of 53BP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C36, C61-74, and C120 demonstrate through genetic rescue experiments that deletion of Trp53 or Chek2 restores brain weight, cortex size, cortical thickness, and reduces apoptosis in Smc5 cKO mice. The rescue is substantial though not always complete for Chek2 deletion. RAD51 upregulation and p53 activation are observed in Smc5 cKO cortices. The lack of rescue with Trp53bp1 deletion provides epistasis information. The convergent genetic and molecular evidence strongly supports the CHEK2-p53 pathway as the primary mediator of the phenotype.

results.result: SMC5 depletion causes abnormal cortical development with ectopic localization of SOX2+ and PAX6+ NPCs outside the VZ, reduction in TBR2+ IPs, and decreased numbers of cortical layer-specific neurons (TBR1+, CTIP2+, SATB2+). Deletion of Trp53 or Chek2 rescues IP and neuron numbers but exacerbates NPC mislocalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-85, C115-116 provide comprehensive immunohistochemical analysis of cortical progenitors and neurons across multiple markers. The data show consistent patterns: Smc5 cKO causes NPC displacement and loss of IPs and neurons, while Trp53 or Chek2 deletion restores IP and neuron populations but worsens NPC positioning. The differential rescue effects suggest distinct mechanisms for apoptosis versus differentiation/positioning defects. The quantifications are statistically significant and internally consistent.

results.result: Smc5 cKO cortices show reduced proliferation with 20.2% fewer Ki67+ cells, 35.7% fewer H3P+ mitotic cells, and 34.7% fewer CldU+ S-phase cells compared to controls. The disproportionate reduction in S-phase and mitotic cells indicates G1 phase accumulation, consistent with a G1 checkpoint activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-88 and C103 provide quantitative cell cycle analysis showing coordinated reductions in proliferation markers. The interpretation that cells accumulate in G1 phase (C88) is supported by the greater reduction in S-phase (34.7%) and mitotic (35.7%) populations compared to total proliferating cells (20.2%). This pattern is consistent with G1 checkpoint activation. The mESC data (C103) showing 1.5-fold increase in G1 cells and 1.5-fold decrease in S/G2 cells after IAA treatment corroborates this interpretation.

results.result: Smc5 cKO NPCs exhibit increased DNA replication stress at pericentromeric heterochromatin, evidenced by 6.5-fold increase in total FANCD2+ foci and 8.1-fold increase in pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci. Pericentromeric H4K20 methylation is reduced by 1.3-fold in width and 2.0-fold in intensity, suggesting under-replicated DNA and DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-94 and C96-97 provide convergent evidence for replication stress at pericentromeric regions using two independent markers: FANCD2 accumulation (a marker of replication stress) and reduced H4K20 methylation (associated with DNA damage and under-replication). The preferential accumulation of FANCD2 at pericentromeric regions (8.1-fold vs 6.5-fold overall) is consistent with these late-replicating regions being particularly vulnerable. The interpretation linking reduced H4K20me to under-replicated DNA (C97) is reasonable given the literature cited.

results.result: In the mESC AID system, SMC5 depletion triggers rapid p53 activation (acetyl-p53 by 2 hr, phospho-p53 by 48 hr) and cell growth arrest. CHEK2 inhibition, but not CHEK1 inhibition, rescues the growth defect. p-p53 accumulates primarily in G1 and prophase cells, with DDR occurring nearly immediately upon SMC5 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-106 and C121 provide detailed kinetics and cell cycle analysis of the DDR in mESCs. The temporal sequence (SMC5 depletion by 1 hr, acetyl-p53 by 2 hr, phospho-p53 by 48 hr) is well-documented. The rescue by CHEK2 but not CHEK1 inhibition (C104-105) is consistent with the in vivo genetic rescue data. The cell cycle distribution of p-p53+ cells (C101-102) supports G1 and prophase checkpoint activation. The interpretation that DDR occurs 'nearly immediately' (C121) is justified by the 2 hr acetyl-p53 upregulation.

results.result: DNA fiber assays in CHEK2-inhibited mESCs show that SMC5 depletion causes replication fork instability: 1.5-fold decrease in ongoing forks, 1.6-fold increase in converging forks, 2.2-fold increase in stalled forks, 1.3-fold reduced track length, and 1.5-fold elevated CldU/IdU ratio. This contrasts with prior studies in cancer cells and may reflect higher intrinsic replication stress in stem cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-109 provide quantitative DNA fiber data showing multiple indicators of replication stress. The use of CHEK2 inhibition to prevent cell death is appropriate for isolating replication defects. Claims C114, C127-132 contextualize these findings relative to prior work, noting that cancer cells (HCT116, RPE1) did not show replication defects, while yeast showed defects only under exogenous stress. The interpretation that mESCs/NPCs have higher intrinsic replication stress (C131-132) is supported by citations showing shorter cell cycle duration. The data are internally consistent and the interpretation is reasonable.

results.result: SMC5-depleted mESCs exhibit increased mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS), with 3.6-fold increase in EdU+ foci and 4.3-fold increase in EdU+FANCD2+ foci per chromosome. MiDAS is particularly elevated at pericentromeric regions (4.7-fold increase in EdU+CEN+ foci, 6.2-fold in EdU+FANCD2+CEN+ foci), with enrichment of acrocentric EdU foci.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-113 provide comprehensive MiDAS analysis using synchronized mESCs with EdU labeling during mitosis. The quantifications show consistent increases across multiple markers (EdU alone, EdU+FANCD2, EdU+CEN, EdU+FANCD2+CEN), with preferential accumulation at pericentromeric regions. The acrocentric/non-acrocentric ratio analysis (C113) provides additional support for pericentromeric enrichment. The data are internally consistent and the methodology (G2 arrest with RO3306, mitotic arrest with STLC, EdU labeling) is appropriate for detecting MiDAS.

results.result: SMC5/6 is required for completion of DNA replication prior to mitosis, particularly at late-replicating regions like pericentromeric heterochromatin. SMC5/6 depletion leads to replication stress, under-replicated DNA persisting into mitosis, chromosome segregation defects, and CHEK2-mediated DDR with p53-dependent apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-6, C37, C114, C141, C143-145 represent the major mechanistic conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental systems: (1) increased FANCD2 and MiDAS at pericentromeric regions in both NPCs and mESCs, (2) DNA fiber assays showing replication fork instability, (3) CldU labeling showing under-replicated DNA in mitotic NPCs, (4) chromosome segregation defects in NPCs, and (5) genetic rescue by Trp53/Chek2 deletion. The model integrates findings across in vivo and in vitro systems and is consistent with the data presented.

results.result: SMC5/6 functions are critical in highly proliferative stem cells during organism development. Conditional knockout in the developing cortex does not affect embryonic survival but causes persistent neurodevelopmental defects into adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C117 represent broad conclusions about SMC5/6 function in development. These are supported by the observation that tissue-specific (Nestin-Cre, Emx1-Cre) but not germline deletion allows survival to adulthood (C52, C117), the demonstration of defects in both NPCs and mESCs (highly proliferative stem cells), and the persistence of cortical defects from embryonic stages through aged adulthood (C59). The conclusion is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Smc5 cKO NPCs do not accumulate in S phase or undergo mitotic delay, indicating that ATR-CHEK1 S phase checkpoint and G2/M checkpoint are not activated. Instead, p53 phosphorylation during prophase may result from late replication defects or under-replicated DNA, while G1 accumulation may result from inheritance of DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-119 are supported by the cell cycle data showing no S-phase accumulation and citation to Phan et al. 2020 for no mitotic delay. However, claims C123-124 are explicitly speculative ('it is conceivable', 'may be caused by') and represent interpretations rather than demonstrated findings. The speculation is reasonable given the data, but these specific mechanisms have not been directly tested. The evaluation is UNCERTAIN because the mechanistic interpretations are plausible but not experimentally validated.

results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-24 represent established background knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.evaluation: Claims C25-33 represent established background knowledge about cortical development and DDR pathways, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Methodological details of the Smc5 cKO mouse model, including the floxed allele design, Cre driver expression patterns, and temporal progression of SMC5/SMC6 protein depletion from E13.5 to E16.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-45 describe the experimental system and are supported by the genotyping PCR (C38, Figure 1A-B), Western blots (C43-44, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B and Figure 1A-C), and citations for Cre driver expression (C40-42). The observation that protein depletion is partial at E13.5 but substantial at E16.5 is important for interpreting the temporal progression of phenotypes. These methodological claims are well-supported.

results.result: Prior work and literature context on SMC5/6 functions, including RAD51 accumulation in Smc5 cKO MEFs, SMC5/6 localization to pericentromeric heterochromatin, differences between stem cells and cancer cells in DDR responses, and roles in telomere maintenance and DNA repair.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C95, C122, C125-126, C133-140 cite prior work from the authors' lab and others to provide context for the current findings. These are appropriately cited and provide important background for interpreting the results. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.
